issue: The red/blue/green coloring of model names and arrows is not explained by a legend or caption. The colors are decorative/redundant but may imply an unstated category, and they collapse in grayscale.
evidence: Figure A.2 uses red for DeepSeek V4-Flash, blue for DeepSeek V4-Pro, green for GLM-5.3-Flash; no legend defines these colors.
acceptance_test: Remove the color coding or add a legend that states its meaning; confirm no information is lost in grayscale.

issue: The top-left box labels AWQ/GPTQ as an 'Error-control method'. AWQ and GPTQ are post-training quantization algorithms, not merely error-control methods. The label is defensible as a shorthand for calibration-guided error reduction, but it is less precise than the rest of the figure and may teach a misleading category.
evidence: Box text: 'Error-control method / AWQ / GPTQ / Calibration guides error reduction'. Caption: 'Quantization choices and execution paths: error-control method, numerical representation, packed tensors and checkpoint container describe different parts of a deployment...'
acceptance_test: Rename the box to 'Quantization method / calibration' or 'Scale/error calibration method' and keep AWQ/GPTQ as examples. The figure should distinguish quantization algorithm from numerical representation without implying AWQ/GPTQ are only error-control mechanisms.

issue: The y-axis label 'Achievable performance' conflicts with the caption's statement that the ceilings are 'peak/theoretical datasheet values, not achieved rates.' A reader can reasonably read 'achievable' as measured or attainable in practice, which is exactly the misconception the caption tries to prevent.
evidence: Y-axis: 'Achievable performance (TFLOPS) — per GPU.' Caption: 'the ceilings are peak/theoretical datasheet values, not achieved rates (sustained MFU is 30–40%, §8.3).' The chart's plateau is a theoretical roofline bound, not an achieved rate.
acceptance_test: Change the y-axis label to 'Theoretical peak performance (TFLOPS)' or 'Roofline bound (TFLOPS)' and ensure the caption and axis use the same scope. Recheck that no prose elsewhere calls the plateau an achieved rate.

issue: The legend contains the sentence 'Token partitioning adds communication between devices,' but no visual symbol or annotation depicts token partitioning or inter-device communication. The legend is therefore carrying prose that does not explain any visual encoding.
evidence: Legend text: 'Solid: data/state flow. Dashed: denoiser conditioning. Blue: data/state. Orange: compute. Token partitioning adds communication between devices.' No box, arrow, or symbol in the diagram represents token partitioning or communication.
acceptance_test: Either add a visual symbol/annotation for token partitioning and inter-device communication, or move the sentence to the caption as a scope note. The legend should contain only keys that map to visible encodings.

figure: Figure 9.1 — Ring traffic and directional bandwidth
issue: The figure note says 'no offload, latency or overlap', but the plotted 544 ms value depends on concurrent send and receive (overlap of the two directions). The note can therefore be read as contradicting the model used to produce the curve.
evidence: Caption: 'Each rank sends 1.75 times the logical tensor size and receives the same amount. Curves use 450 GB/s ...'. Prose on printed p. 156: 'With concurrent send and receive, its ideal time is T_ring ≈ 245/450 ≈ 0.54 s. Equivalently, 490 GB of sent-plus-received traffic divided by 900 GB/s gives the same time.' Figure note: 'Analytical model; no offload, latency or overlap; not measured.' If 'overlap' meant no send/receive overlap, the time would be 490/450 ≈ 1.09 s, not 0.54 s.
acceptance_test: Revise the note to say 'no offload, latency, or communication/computation overlap' (or equivalent), so it cannot be read as denying the concurrent send/receive assumption behind the plotted times.

figure: Figure 9.1 — Ring traffic and directional bandwidth
issue: The caption does not state the time formula used for the curves. A reader can see 'sent bytes per rank = 1.75 × tensor bytes' and 'ideal ring completion time' but is not told that the plotted time is sent bytes per rank divided by directional bandwidth, with send and receive concurrent.
evidence: Subtitle: 'sent bytes per rank = 1.75 × tensor bytes'. Caption: 'Each rank sends 1.75 times the logical tensor size and receives the same amount. Curves use 450 GB/s ...'. The caption never says 'time = sent bytes per rank / directional bandwidth' or 'assuming concurrent send and receive'. The prose on p. 156 supplies this, but the figure caption should be self-contained.
acceptance_test: Add one clause to the caption: 'Plotted time is sent bytes per rank divided by directional bandwidth, assuming concurrent send and receive.'

issue: The figure says 'Balanced ring neighbor order (both phases)' and shows R0→R1→R2→R3→R0, but it does not show which 2 B chunk each rank sends in each round. For a reader trying to reconstruct the ring algorithm, the diagram shows the neighbor order but not the chunk rotation that makes reduce-scatter and all-gather work.
evidence: Figure text: 'Balanced ring neighbor order (both phases)' with R0→R1→R2→R3→R0. Below: 'Each round sends one 2 B chunk to the next rank.' The figure does not label the chunks (e.g., chunk 0, chunk 1, chunk 2, chunk 3) or show which chunk moves in round 1, 2, 3. The caption says 'Reduce-scatter leaves one reduced element per rank; all-gather then replicates the already-reduced fragments', but the chunk rotation is left implicit.
acceptance_test: Either add small chunk labels (0/1/2/3) to the ring arrows or add one sentence to the caption: 'In round r, rank i sends chunk (i−r) mod N; the same rotation is used in both phases.'

figure: Figure 9.3 — The payload path is not the bootstrap path
issue: The figure's right-hand path places 'Plugin: MPI or OFI' under '3 Device runtime plus transport', while the bottom note says 'GPU-aware MPI can carry payload too; MPI is not CPU-only.' The diagram therefore shows MPI in two different roles (setup/control and transport/plugin) without visually distinguishing those roles.
evidence: Top dashed box: 'Launcher, rank/device mapping, rendezvous' with 'MPI or a store can distribute communicator IDs.' Right path under '3 Device runtime plus transport': 'SYCL / Level Zero path / Plugin: MPI or OFI / Actual path depends on build'. Bottom note: 'GPU-aware MPI can carry payload too; MPI is not CPU-only.' Caption: 'Dashed setup connections do not imply that MPI carries the collective payload; GPU-aware MPI is also a possible payload implementation.' The figure uses the same word 'MPI' for setup and for a possible transport/plugin without a visual or textual role distinction.
acceptance_test: Either label the right-path MPI entry as 'MPI transport (payload-capable)' or add a caption sentence: 'MPI appears in two roles: setup/rendezvous (dashed) and, in some builds, payload transport (solid); the figure does not imply they are the same path.'

issue: The all-reduce arrow originates only from GPU 0, while the label says 'all-reduce partial sums'; the figure does not show GPU 1 contributing to the collective.
evidence: Panel A shows a single red arrow from the bottom of GPU 0 to the red dashed 'all-reduce partial sums → full output' box; no corresponding arrow from GPU 1. The label and caption describe a collective over both GPUs' partial sums.
acceptance_test: Add a second arrow from GPU 1 to the all-reduce box, or draw a bidirectional/collective arrow between both GPUs and the box; verify the visual is symmetric and matches the all-reduce semantics.

issue: The annotation 'a finishing sequence frees its slot immediately' points to the green backfill segment, not to the end of the finishing blue sequence or the freed-slot boundary.
evidence: The arrow from the annotation terminates on the narrow green bar in the top row. The finishing sequence is the blue bar immediately to its left; the green bar is the new sequence that fills the freed slot.
acceptance_test: Redirect the arrow to the boundary between the finishing blue sequence and the green backfill, or reword the annotation to 'a freed slot is refilled immediately' and keep the arrow on the green segment. Verify the annotation's subject and arrow target agree.

issue: Panel A shows four prefill GPUs and four decode GPUs but a single KV arrow labeled '450 GB/s per GPU per direction'; the caveat compares aggregate 1.4 TB/s to 'any single link above' without noting the four-link aggregate (4 × 450 GB/s = 1.8 TB/s). evidence: Panel A: '8× H100 host' with 4 orange prefill GPUs and 4 blue decode GPUs; one red KV arrow labeled '450 GB/s per GPU per direction'. Caveat: '35 GB/request × 40 req/s = 1.4 TB/s of payload' and '1.4 TB/s exceeds any single link above.' The panel's four NVLink links aggregate to ~1.8 TB/s, which exceeds 1.4 TB/s.
acceptance_test: Label the arrow with the aggregate capacity (e.g., '4 × 450 GB/s = 1.8 TB/s aggregate') or draw multiple links; clarify in the caveat that 1.4 TB/s exceeds one link but not necessarily the four-link aggregate. Verify the figure does not imply the NVLink case is infeasible at the stated load.

issue: The Outcome box says 'CLEARS CAPACITY GATE (a) · (b)' while the caption says the three candidates are 'conditional', each has an 'open validation gate (not a settled verdict)', and 'no candidate is deployment-validated'. issue: The row labels say 'Prefill hosts, avg 92K tok/s' and 'Prefill hosts, peak 368K tok/s', but column (c) reports '~4 H100 cards' and '~15 H100 cards'. issue: The x-axis label says 'duration varied at FIXED 40 rps peak, FIXED 21-host fleet', but the vertical 'feasible max 24.96M' line assumes the canonical 624,000 active-s/mo duty cycle. If the reader interprets 'duration varied' as varying the active window, the fixed feasible-max line appears inconsistent. The caption and printed p. 268 clarify that only load duration within the fixed active window varies, but the axis label alone is ambiguous.
evidence: X-axis label: 'Requests/month (log) — duration varied at FIXED 40 rps peak, FIXED 21-host fleet'; annotation: 'feasible max 24.96M'; caption: 'feasible max = capacity 40 rps × 624,000 s = 24.96M req/mo'; printed p. 268: 'only how long the peak-shaped load runs inside the active window moves along x'.
acceptance_test: Revise the x-axis label to make the fixed active window explicit, e.g. 'Requests/month (log) — load duration varied within the fixed 624,000 s active window; 40 rps peak; 21-host fleet'. Alternatively, if the active window is meant to vary, replace the single feasible-max line with a duration-dependent bound.

issue: The annotation 'one-host cannot meet the burst on its own' points to a low-load part of the red curve, not the burst peak.

issue: Grayscale distinguishability is weak: the thin gray dashed one-host bound sits inside the light red shaded area, and both the blue capacity line and gray one-host line are dashed.
evidence: The gray dashed line at y≈2.0 runs through the red fill; in grayscale the fill becomes light gray and the line medium gray. The blue dashed capacity line and gray dashed one-host line share a dash pattern, differing mainly by weight/position.

evidence: The orange N-1 residual line is at ~6.0 req/s; 'headroom' sits above it at ~6.3 and 'failover' below it at ~5.2, while the burst peak is ~5.5 and the N=4 capacity is ~8.0. The reader cannot tell whether headroom means burst-to-N-1, N-1-to-N=4, or something else.

issue: Color coding is unexplained and inconsistent with the caption's family categories: 'Small gen' and 'General' are both green although the caption distinguishes general-purpose and fallback families, while 'Fallthrough' is orange and 'Frontier' is teal.
evidence: No legend defines the colors. The leaves use blue (specialist), teal (Frontier), green (Small gen), and green (General); the intermediate 'Fallthrough' box is orange. A reader may infer that Small gen and General are the same category, or that Fallthrough is a model family.

issue: Legend order does not match the stacked-bar order in panel (a).

figure: Figure 22.1 — Attention vs. projection prefill FLOP crossover
issue: The left panel's x-axis ends at 100K tokens, but the annotated causal-triangle crossover is at ~106.8K tokens. The crossing is therefore outside the plotted range, and the annotation arrow points to the green curve near the right edge rather than to a visible intersection.
evidence: Left panel x-axis ticks are 10^0, 10^1, 10^2 K tokens, i.e. 1K, 10K, 100K. The annotation says 'causal-triangle: crossover ~106.8K'. The green and red curves do not visibly cross within the plotted domain; the arrow points to the green curve at approximately 100K.
acceptance_test: Extend the left panel x-axis to at least 200K tokens (or add an inset) so the ~106.8K crossing is visible, or explicitly mark the crossover with an off-axis arrow and state that it lies just beyond the plotted range. figure: Figure 21.1 — AI Factory promotion: a measured gate on each transition
issue: The caption says production feedback returns evidence to 'data/evaluation', and the bottom label says 'production feedback -> data / evaluation', but the green feedback line in the diagram appears to return only to the Data stage. There is no visible branch or arrow into Eval.

page_hint: Ch 1, §1 Concept, 'Tokenization' paragraph, first sentence
quoted_clause: or in worst cases a fragment of a character
observed: The phrase 'a fragment of a character' is technically correct (a single byte of a multi-byte UTF-8 codepoint) but may lead a reader to think the tokenizer splits individual characters into sub-character pieces. The subsequent BPE description ('byte-pair encoding (BPE) repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent byte/subword pairs') clarifies the byte-level operation, but the initial list of token types could be more precise.
evidence: BPE operates on bytes. A 'token' in the worst case is a single byte, which for a multi-byte UTF-8 character (e.g., a 4-byte emoji) is indeed a fragment of that character. But the phrasing 'fragment of a character' without the byte-level qualifier could be misread as 'a piece of a letter' in a character-level sense.
root_cause: The list is written from the reader's perspective (what the token looks like) rather than the implementation perspective (what the tokenizer produces). The byte-level mechanism is explained two sentences later.
correction: Change to 'or in worst cases a single byte (which for multi-byte Unicode characters is a fragment of a character)'. This preserves the reader-facing intuition while anchoring it to the byte-level mechanism that the BPE description will elaborate.
acceptance_test:
A reader who stops after the first sentence and does not read the BPE paragraph still understands that the worst-case token is a byte, not an arbitrary sub-character slice."
  }

page_hint: Ch 3, §1 Concept, 'Alternative inference' subsection (from 'From corruption to learned generation' through 'State reuse follows dependency boundaries')
quoted_clause: This subsection and the three that follow cover the alternative-inference thread — diffusion/LLaDA-style generation where the token is not the execution step. It is the book's coverage of the 2026 alternative-inference frontier; the core dense/MoE/KV thread resumes in §2 (Mental Model).
observed: The alternative-inference section is approximately 2,500 words of dense technical content (diffusion, flow matching, masked language models, block-causal models, cache invalidation under bidirectional attention) inserted between the dense/MoE concept and the mental model. While the 'Reader orientation' note tells the reader they can skip, the section's length and density create a significant interruption to the main thread. A reader who does not skip must hold the diffusion material in working memory while also tracking the dense/MoE argument that resumes in §2.
evidence: The section covers: continuous denoising diffusion, score-based SDEs, discrete diffusion (MDLM, LLaDA), flow matching, rectified flow, masked language sampling, parallel prediction, agent-loop distinction, state reuse under bidirectional attention, block-causal models, DiffusionGemma, LLaDA2.2, and Wan2.2 A14B. That is at least 8 distinct technical topics in one subsection.
root_cause: The book wants to cover the 2026 alternative-inference frontier without creating a separate chapter (which would break the token→fleet spine). Placing it in Ch 3 (model understanding) is the right location, but the delivery as a single continuous subsection is too dense for the main reading path.
correction: Add a 3–4 sentence summary at the end of the section that states the key architectural consequence for the main thread (e.g., 'The one point that carries forward: in diffusion/alternative inference, the execution unit is a model evaluation over a canvas, not a token; the total-vs-active and KV-residency frameworks of this chapter still apply, but the per-token accounting must be replaced by per-evaluation accounting. The full treatment is Ch 27 and Appendix A.'). This gives the non-skipping reader a clean exit point and a bridge back to the main thread without requiring them to hold all 8 topics in memory.
acceptance_test:
A reader who finishes the alternative-inference section can state in one sentence what it means for the dense/MoE framework before reading §2. The section has a clear 'so what for the main thread' conclusion."
  }

page_hint: Ch 2, §2 Mental Model, prefill/decode water metaphor
quoted_clause: It is like pushing the water of that same 140 GB reservoir through a standard garden hose: the whole volume must flow every 25 milliseconds just to deliver one glass of water — one generated token.
observed: The metaphor frames the 140 GB as a 'reservoir' of water that must be pushed through a hose. In the actual mechanism, the 140 GB is the weight matrix stored in HBM, and the 'hose' is the HBM-to-SM data path. The metaphor is effective for the bandwidth-bound intuition, but 'reservoir' subtly implies a volume of fluid being consumed, whereas the weights are re-read (not consumed) every step. A careful reader might wonder whether the 140 GB is 'used up' after one token.
evidence: The text immediately after the metaphor says 'the pump (compute) is more than powerful enough, but the diameter of the hose (HBM bandwidth) physically cannot move that volume of water in that time frame.' The 'move that volume' phrasing is correct (the data is moved, not consumed). But 'reservoir' + 'pushing the water' could imply consumption.
root_cause: The water metaphor is a standard and effective analogy for bandwidth-bound vs compute-bound. The 'reservoir' framing is a minor imprecision in an otherwise clear analogy.
correction: Optional: change 'pushing the water of that same 140 GB reservoir through a standard garden hose' to 'streaming the full 140 GB of weight data through a standard garden hose (HBM bandwidth) every 25 milliseconds'. This removes the 'reservoir' (implies a tank being drained) and makes the re-read nature explicit. Alternatively, add a half-sentence: 'The reservoir is not drained — the same 140 GB is re-read every step, but the hose is too narrow to move it in 25 ms.'

page_hint: Ch 6, §3, 'Reading Telemetry Into a Decision' paragraph
quoted_clause: each ~1.29 PFLOP — aggregate prefill demand at the 40 rps peak is 40 × 1.29 ≈ 52 PFLOP/s
observed: The 1.29 PFLOP figure is the case-(i) linear-only prefill FLOP count. Chapter 8's explicit convention states: 'every prefill FLOP figure and every prefill host count states which case it uses.' This occurrence in Ch 6 does not label the case. The same figure appears in Ch 6's mini-case ('repeated full 9.2K prefills') without a case label.
evidence: Ch 8 §3: 'Chapters 8, 15, 16, 17, 20 and 22 name the same three cases, and every prefill FLOP figure and every prefill host count states which case it uses.' The 1.29 value matches case (i) (1.288 PFLOP rounded).
root_cause: The Ch 6 text was written before or independently of the Ch 8 three-case convention and was not updated to add the case label.
correction: Add a brief parenthetical: 'each ~1.29 PFLOP (case (i), linear-only; the full-square case (ii) gives ~1.51 PFLOP, raising the oversubscription ratio to ~21×)'. Alternatively, since the point is a rough 'several times past capacity' argument, add '(linear-only approximation; see Ch 8 §3 for the three-case accounting)'.
acceptance_test: Every prefill FLOP figure in Ch 6 carries an explicit case label or a pointer to the Ch 8 convention.

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a), 'Takeaway for the canonical RAG workload'
quoted_clause: the bge-large-en option is overkill for this scale
observed: 'Overkill' is informal register for a technical architecture handbook. The surrounding sentence provides the quantitative reasoning (unquantified quality gain must clear a ~3× FLOP bar), so the word is doing no additional work beyond the reasoning.
evidence: The sentence continues: 'its quality gain over all-mpnet-base-v2 is not quantified for this model pair (the table gives use cases, not metrics), and an unquantified gain would have to clear a ~3× FLOP bar (≈43 vs ≈14 GFLOPs per 64-token embedding in the table above, the same ratio as their parameter counts) — validate the gain on the target corpus before paying it.' The quantitative argument is complete without 'overkill.'
root_cause: Colloquial phrasing slipped into a formal recommendation paragraph.
correction: Replace 'is overkill for this scale' with 'is not justified at this scale' or 'exceeds what this workload's compute budget warrants without a quantified quality gain.'
acceptance_test: The sentence reads at the same register as the surrounding technical prose.

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(c), the Q* formula scope note
quoted_clause: (Scope: this Q* amortizes only the one-time training + carry cost against the quality uplift; it omits the recurring per-query prefill/retrieval saving that fine-tuning's shorter context (§5.3(c)) would confer, so it is a lower bound on the fine-tuning case and overstates the break-even volume.)
observed: The scope limitation is important (the formula is not the full economic comparison) but is buried in a long parenthetical at the end of a dense paragraph. A reader who skims the paragraph may miss it and treat Q* as the complete break-even criterion.
evidence: The parenthetical is 45 words and contains a cross-reference (§5.3(c)) and a directional claim ('lower bound on the fine-tuning case and overstates the break-even volume'). The main text before it says 'The economic comparison should be framed parametrically, not with a single number, because the break-even depends on the quality uplift (domain-specific) and the query volume (workload-specific).' The scope note adds a further limitation not captured by that sentence.
root_cause: The scope note was added as a post-hoc clarification rather than integrated into the main argument structure.
correction: Promote the scope note to a standalone sentence immediately after the formula, before the 'Below Q*' explanation: 'Note: this formula captures only the one-time training and carry cost amortized against the quality uplift. It does not include the recurring per-query savings from a shorter fine-tuned context (less retrieval, less prefill), which would lower the true break-even volume. The Q* above is therefore a conservative (higher) estimate of the queries needed to justify fine-tuning.'
acceptance_test: A reader who stops after the formula and the 'Below Q*' sentence still understands that the formula is incomplete and in which direction it is incomplete.

page_hint: Ch 7, Fig 7.7 caption and the 'Technical note — per-rank fit' paragraph

page_hint: Ch 6, §3, 'Detecting the Regime' — the decode bandwidth paragraph
quoted_clause: Within a ~25 ms TPOT budget that demands 140 GB / 0.025 s ≈ 5.6 TB/s (batch-1-equivalent) of HBM bandwidth, against an H100's ~3.35 TB/s peak [1P][FACT]. The two scope notes (single-device vs 8×H100; aggregate vs per-rank) are then stated in a dense paragraph. The key insight (decode is bandwidth-bound because of low arithmetic intensity, not because 5.6 > 3.35) is buried at the end of the paragraph.
evidence: The 5.6 TB/s is the aggregate model-wide weight-read rate for a hypothetical single-device implementation. Under TP=8, each GPU reads 140/8 = 17.5 GB per token, requiring 17.5/0.025 = 0.7 TB/s against its 3.35 TB/s — well within capacity. The bandwidth-bound classification follows from the 1.0 FLOP/byte intensity (far below the 295 ridge), not from the 5.6 > 3.35 comparison. The text states all this correctly but in an order that risks the reader anchoring on the 5.6-vs-3.35 number first.

correction: Restructure: (1) State the intensity argument first: 'Decode at batch 1 has an arithmetic intensity of ~1.0 FLOP/byte (140 GFLOP / 140 GB), far below the ~295 FLOP/byte ridge — this is why decode is bandwidth-bound, regardless of how many GPUs are used.' (2) Then give the single-device illustration: 'As a concrete single-device illustration: 140 GB / 0.025 s ≈ 5.6 TB/s exceeds one H100's 3.35 TB/s peak. Under TP=8, each GPU reads only 17.5 GB (0.7 TB/s), so the per-GPU bandwidth is not the binding constraint — the low intensity is.' (3) Then the scope note: 'This is an operating-point property, not an identity: at high batch, decode intensity rises and can approach the ridge.'
acceptance_test: A reader who reads only the first two sentences of the restructured paragraph can state why decode is bandwidth-bound (low intensity) and why the 5.6-vs-3.35 comparison is illustrative rather than verdictal.

issue: Cost-ledger arithmetic is internally inconsistent: the table's parenthetical base and the prose's rounded base both disagree with the table's own printed result and with the prose's unrounded value, so a reader cannot reproduce $0.0076 from the numbers shown next to it.

The prose on the same page reads: 'The hosted-API cost is a separate basis: $0.016/request (unrounded $0.01164 ≈ $11.6 per 1,000 requests, Ch 4)'. Here 0.01164 × 1000 = 11.64 ≈ 11.6 (consistent), but 0.01164 rounds to $0.012, not $0.016. Three per-request values (0.0164, 0.016, 0.01164) are therefore in play, and only 0.01164 reproduces the printed 0.0076. The table's stated multiplier base (0.0164) is the wrong anchor, and the prose's rounded figure ($0.016) is also wrong relative to its own unrounded figure.
acceptance_test: After the edit, recompute and confirm: (a) the table parenthetical reads '$0.01164 × 0.65' (or '$0.012 × 0.65 ≈ $0.0076') so that base × 0.65 = 0.0076; (b) the prose rounded value is '$0.012/request' or the rounded figure is dropped in favor of '$0.01164'; (c) 0.01164 × 0.65 = 0.007566 ≈ 0.0076 and 0.01164 × 1000 = 11.64 ≈ 11.6. All three anchors (table result, table base, prose base) must then agree, and the FACT Target '< $0.015' must still be satisfied by 0.0076.
